newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: European summit promises peace, security ahead.
newsitem.headline: European summit promises peace, security ahead.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

A European security summit ended on Tuesday by promising peace and cooperation to all in the 21st century, but bitter arguments over the protests in Serbia and the problems of former Soviet republics spoiled its vision.

Leaders of the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) agreed to respect democracy and human rights, and pledged more arms control and an end to confrontation on the continent where two world wars started.

"As we approach the new century, it is more important than ever that we build together a peaceful...region where all our nations and individuals feel secure," the leaders said in the two-day summit's final declaration.

"We are determined to learn from the tragedies of the past and to translate our vision of a cooperative future into reality by creating a common security space free of dividing lines in which all states are equal partners."
Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres, who hosted the meeting, urged the leaders to keep their commitments.
"We owe it to our people, who gave us their trust, we owe it to future generations and we owe it to history," he said.

The summit has been marked by Russia's opposition to NATO enlargement and concern over the crisis in Belarus, with leading OSCE states calling on Tuesday for President Alexander Lukashenko to put his country back on the path to democracy.

A row between the former Soviet republics of Armenia and Azerbaijan over the enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh had even threatened to block agreement on the final declaration, which needed the agreement of all countries.
The two countries went to war in 1988 over the issue but have since agreed a ceasefire.

In the end, they agreed to put the row to one side but the debates in Lisbon have underlined how difficult it is to resolve ethnic problems and regional conflicts now that the neat East-West divisions of the Cold War have gone.

Western diplomats said Russia, apparently resentful that it has failed to stop NATO's plans for enlargement, had insisted the declaration remove a call for democracy in Serbia, where President Slobodan Milosevic faces mass protests.

Many leaders in Lisbon had expressed concern that Milosevic, now facing an unprecedented challenge to his nine years of autocratic rule, could use force against protesters now thronging the streets of Belgrade and calling on him to quit.
Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, did not attend the summit because its OSCE membership has been suspended.
But Russia, which has often taken Serbia's side in the Yugoslav conflict, appeared ready to flex its diplomatic muscles in support of Milosevic.
Western diplomats said Russia insisted a phrase from the draft declaration calling for "democratisation, independent media, free and fair elections" in Serbia was removed.
"The Russians have been insistent and eloquent defenders of the unfortunate Yugoslav position," said one diplomat.
Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin had told the summit on Monday that Moscow still opposed NATO plans to take in countries such as Poland and Hungary by the year 2000.
Nevertheless, the summit endorsed the right of all countries to join alliances -- without mentioning NATO by name.

Russia also won little support at the summit for strengthening the OSCE as a counterbalance to the Western alliance but did win agreement on a new round of arms control talks to adapt a Cold War-era agreement on conventional forces.
The last major European security summit, in Budapest in 1994, collapsed in humiliating disarray after a row on the NATO issue and differences over the war in Bosnia.
The disputes in Lisbon, although serious, are not as bitter or threatening -- principally because the war in Bosnia ended last year.
This summit approved a continued role for the OSCE in Bosnia next year, working alongside the NATO-led peace force and supervising local elections.
The OSCE's Bosnia operation builds on its role as a monitor of democracy, human rights and arms control. The forum has its roots in a 1975 East-West conference in Helsinki.
In other developments on Tuesday, Germany and the Czech Republic said they were hopeful a dispute over ethnic Germans expelled from part of Czechoslovakia after World War Two would be resolved soon.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl met Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus on the margins of the summit.
